610.title: I am the bread of life (John 6:22–51)
610.hook: the first I AM: whoever comes to me will never hunger
610.howItsDone: Christians often connect this saying with communion; in many churches, the bread is shared at the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist or Holy Communion, and many Christians also say grace before ordinary meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a voice on the water in the dark: ego eimi, it is I. Your line was be not afraid.

Next morning, the crowd from the hillside wakes up and Jesus is gone. So are the disciples. They grab whatever boats they can find and cross the lake to Capernaum looking for him. When they find him, he doesn't say welcome. He says, gently but plainly: you're not here because of the signs. You're here because you ate the bread and were filled. People come back to the place they last got fed. Who doesn't? Then he tells them what he's really offering.

"Labour not for the meat which perisheth," he says: food that goes stale. Work for food that lasts. The crowd brings up their history: "Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat." Manna fell every morning in the wilderness, enough for one day, never more. Can you top that? Jesus says the true bread from heaven isn't something Moses gave; it's something the Father gives now. And the crowd, like the woman at the well asking for that water, says: "Lord, evermore give us this bread." Then he says it: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." It's the first of seven great sayings in John where Jesus says I am and names a picture: bread, light, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection, the way, the vine. We'll meet every one on this path. Bread was the plainest thing on any table in that world, the food of every family, rich and poor. He doesn't say I am a feast, or a rare delicacy. He says I am bread: something you need daily, that keeps you alive. Christians understand this in different ways. Many hear it about faith: coming to Jesus feeds a hunger nothing else fills. Catholic and Orthodox Christians, with many others, also hear the bread of communion. Many hear both at once. And the word he keeps returning to is life.
screen: `THE FIRST OF SEVEN I AM SAYINGS.`
then, large: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: If you have a piece of bread or a cracker nearby, take it; if not, picture one, and think of the field, the wheat, the person who baked it. Take one small bite and chew slowly, longer than feels normal, noticing the simple fact of being fed. Then ask what you're hungry for that bread can't fill: if you pray, bring that hunger to God, and if you don't, give thanks for the bread.
Bread. The everyday food Jesus named himself as, the first of his seven I am sayings in John: whoever comes to him will never hunger.
Your line: bread of life. Daily bread, plain and needed, not a rare feast. See you tomorrow.

611.title: To whom shall we go? (John 6:52–71)
611.hook: many leave; Peter says: you have the words of eternal life
611.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Peter's words in seasons of doubt, and in some liturgies his line is sung as a verse before the Gospel is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna, and a plain claim: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life.

There's a moment in a lot of friendships, and a lot of faiths, when the thing gets hard. Something is said that you can't quite follow, or can't quite accept. You look around, and other people are quietly leaving. This is that moment in John's Gospel. In the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus's teaching about bread from heaven gets stranger and stronger, and even his own followers mutter among themselves: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?"

What was so hard? Jesus had said that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. His hearers take it as literally as anyone would, and they recoil. Christians have understood these words in different ways ever since. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hear in them the Eucharist, the bread and wine that become, in their teaching, the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Other Protestant churches read the words as a picture of faith: taking Christ in, the way bread is taken into the body. In the story, the result is the same: "From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him." Not enemies. Disciples. So Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will ye also go away?" He doesn't beg them to stay. He doesn't soften what he said. He just asks. And Peter answers for them: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Listen to how honest that is. Peter doesn't say I understand everything, or it was easy to hear. He says, where else would we go? It isn't certainty. It's a choice about where life is, made on a day he doesn't understand everything. And John adds a sad note: Jesus already knows one of the twelve will betray him.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?`

segments.voice: Think of something that gives you life but has gotten hard lately: a friendship, a marriage, a practice like this one, a faith if you have one. Notice whether part of you wants to walk away quietly, and without scolding it, ask Peter's question: if I leave, where would I go? If you pray, tell God plainly what's hard; if you don't, hold the thing that gives you life, and choose it for today.
Peter. The one who answered for the twelve when many disciples left: Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life.
Your line: to whom else? It's a question, and an answer. Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: Judge rightly (John 7:1–24)
612.hook: at the harvest festival of booths, he teaches in secret then openly
612.howItsDone: Christians read this chapter as part of John's story of Jesus at the great Jewish feasts; Jews today keep Sukkot each autumn by building and eating in a sukkah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many walked away, and Peter asked: Lord, to whom shall we go? Your line was to whom else?

Each autumn, Jewish families who keep Sukkot build a little hut: walls of wood or cloth, a roof of branches loose enough to see the stars through. For a week they eat in it, and some sleep in it. It's called a sukkah, a booth, and the festival is Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles. Jews still keep it today. Today's chapter of John opens as that feast approaches, and Jesus's own brothers are pushing him: go up to Jerusalem, show yourself to the world.
screen: `A HUT WITH A ROOF OF BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: "Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent. The law of Moses told Israel to live in booths for seven days, remembering the wilderness years, when God's people lived in tents and God kept them. It was a harvest festival too, full of joy. John is honest about family: "For neither did his brethren believe in him." Jesus says his time hasn't come and stays behind. Then, after they leave, he goes up anyway, quietly, not openly. In Jerusalem, people are whispering: he's a good man; no, he's leading people astray. Halfway through the feast, he walks into the temple courts and teaches out loud. People are amazed: "How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?" He hasn't studied under any teacher they know. He's from Galilee. They're judging by appearances, and he knows it. Then he takes up the sabbath healing again. You circumcise a baby boy on the sabbath, he says, when the eighth day falls on it, so the law of Moses isn't broken. Why be angry with me for making a whole man well on the sabbath? It's a careful argument from inside Jewish practice. And he ends: "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." A man from Galilee with no teacher might be a teacher. A healing on the sabbath might be keeping the sabbath, not breaking it.
screen: then, large: `JUDGE NOT ACCORDING TO THE APPEARANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've judged quickly, by their clothes, their accent, their job, or one thing they said. Then imagine what you don't know, what they carry, what they've survived, what they might be good at, and let your picture of them get a little bigger. If you pray, ask to see them as God sees them; if you don't, hold them with more curiosity than you did a minute ago.
Sukkot. The Jewish feast of booths, kept each autumn, that this day's chapter opens as Jerusalem prepares for it.
Your line: judge not by appearance. The surface is only the start of a person. Until tomorrow.

613.title: Rivers of living water (John 7:25–52)
613.hook: on the great day of the feast he cries: let anyone thirsty come
613.howItsDone: Christians often read this passage at Pentecost, connecting the rivers of living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit; many also connect it with baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot, huts with roofs of branches, and a teacher judged by appearances. Your line was judge not by appearance.

A golden pitcher, a pool, and a procession at dawn. According to Jewish tradition written down in the Mishnah, on the mornings of the Feast of Tabernacles a priest walked down to the pool of Siloam, filled a golden pitcher, and carried it back up to the temple, with crowds and music. At the altar, he poured the water out. In a dry land waiting for the winter rains, that poured-out water meant something. Now it's the last day of the feast, the greatest day. And in the middle of the crowds, Jesus stands up and shouts.

"In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." Then: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Belly is the old, literal word. Here it means the deepest inside of a person, which is why some modern translations say heart. And there's a puzzle: whose heart? The sentence can be read two ways: rivers flowing out of the believer, or out of Jesus himself, for anyone who comes and drinks. Readers have taken it both ways. John explains in the next verse: Jesus was speaking about the Spirit, which those who believed would receive. A woman at a well heard about living water. A crowd heard about bread. Now, at a festival of water, Jesus offers rivers. And the crowd splits. Some say he's the prophet, some the Christ. Others say the Christ can't come from Galilee. Officers sent to arrest him come back empty-handed. Why didn't you bring him? "Never man spake like this man." And one quiet voice on the council speaks up: Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter three. Shouldn't we hear a man before judging him? He's beginning to come out of the dark.

If you have a glass of water near you, hold it; if not, picture one, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, pipes under your street, the people who keep them working. Take a slow sip and notice that your body needed it, even if you didn't feel thirsty. If you pray, give thanks for the water; if you don't, give thanks for the glass in your hand.
Belly. The old, literal word for the deepest inside of a person: out of it, Jesus said, would flow rivers of living water.
Your line: out of the heart, rivers. The old word was belly. That's day six hundred thirteen.

614.title: Let the one without sin (John 8:1–11)
614.hook: a woman dragged before him; he writes in the dust; stones fall; a passage later manuscripts added
614.howItsDone: Christians often read this story when teaching about mercy and judging others; some churches read it during Lent, and "cast the first stone" has passed into everyday English.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a festival of water, and Jesus crying out: rivers of living water. Your line was out of the heart, rivers.

Early morning in the temple courts. Jesus is sitting, teaching a crowd. A group of men push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone. She's been caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. Moses commanded that such should be stoned. What do you say? It's a trap. If he says let her go, he seems to set aside the law. If he says stone her, the teacher of mercy approves an execution. The woman stands there, alone. And Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger.

"But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not." What did he write? The Gospel never says. Readers have guessed for centuries: the sins of the accusers, a verse from the prophets, nothing at all. They keep pressing. So he stands and says one sentence: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he writes again. And one by one they leave, "beginning at the eldest, even unto the last." The oldest first, maybe because they had the longest memories of their own failures. Notice what the story leaves out. The law named both the man and the woman. Where is he? When they've all gone, Jesus speaks to her directly, maybe the first person that morning to do so. "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?" She said, "No man, Lord." "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." Both halves matter: no condemnation, and a new way to live. A scholar's detail: a modern Bible may print this story in brackets, noting that the oldest Greek copies of John don't have it, and later copies place it in different spots, some even in Luke. Some readers think it's an old story about Jesus that circulated on its own before finding a home in the Gospel. The Catholic Church holds it as part of scripture, and Protestant and Orthodox churches read and preach it too.

segments.voice: Think of someone you're holding a stone against, someone who hurt you or failed you; you don't have to forgive them completely today. Remember one of your own failures, something you'd hate dragged into the middle of a crowd, and if you can, set the stone down, even for a few minutes. If you pray, ask for help to leave it there; if you don't, notice how your hand feels empty.

615.title: The light of the world (John 8:12–30)
615.hook: whoever follows me won't walk in darkness
615.tomorrow: the truth will set you free
615.howItsDone: Many Christians light candles in worship as a sign of Christ as the light of the world; at the Easter Vigil in many churches, a single candle is carried into a dark church and its flame is shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, words written in the dust, and stones set down one by one. Your line was neither do I condemn you.

Jerusalem had no streetlights. After sunset there were oil lamps, the moon, and not much else. Then, one week a year, the temple lit up. According to the Mishnah, at the Feast of Tabernacles huge golden lampstands stood in the temple's Court of the Women, and young priests climbed ladders to fill their bowls with oil. Wicks were made from the priests' worn-out garments. The tradition says there wasn't a courtyard in Jerusalem that wasn't lit by that light, and people danced with torches beneath it all night. In that same court, Jesus speaks.

"I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." Bread first, now light: the second of the I am sayings in John. And John says exactly where: "These words spake Jesus in the treasury, as he taught in the temple." The treasury, where the offering chests stood, was in the Court of the Women, where those great lamps burned at the feast. So he's there, near the lampstands, saying: I am the light. Light has run through John since its first lines: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness could not grasp it or put it out. Now the light speaks for itself. Notice the shape of the promise. He doesn't say whoever follows me will never face darkness. Night still comes. He says they won't walk in darkness; they'll carry the light of life, like someone walking home at night with a lamp. The path isn't lit all the way to the end, just enough for the next step. The listeners push back: you're testifying about yourself; that doesn't count. Jesus answers that his Father bears witness with him. Who are you? He speaks of a day when they'll lift up the Son of Man, a hint of the cross, and then they'll know. John ends simply: as he spoke these words, many believed in him.

segments.voice: Turn toward a window, a lamp, or the brightest thing in the room, and if you can, take a few slow steps toward it. Light. The second of Jesus's I am sayings in John, spoken where the great festival lamps burned: whoever follows carries the light of life.

616.title: The truth will set you free (John 8:31–59)
616.carry: the truth shall make you free
616.howItsDone: Christians read this passage as teaching that freedom comes from staying with Jesus's word; churches today also teach clearly against using John 8 to blame or demean Jewish people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, golden lamps in the temple, and Jesus saying: I am the light of the world. Your line was the light of life.

Some sentences escape their books. This one is carved in stone in the lobby of the CIA's original headquarters building in Virginia. It's on university buildings and library walls. In Latin, it's the motto of Johns Hopkins University. Politicians quote it, journalists quote it, people who've never opened a Bible quote it. "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Out of context, it sounds like a slogan for information: get the facts and you'll be free. But in John it's the middle of a hard conversation, and the sentence before it changes everything.

Here's the sentence before: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed." Continue means stay, abide, live there. So this truth isn't a fact you look up. You come to know it by staying close to him, the way you only really know a friend after years together. And the freedom isn't political. His hearers object: "We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man." Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin. The freedom he offers works from the inside out. The argument gets sharp, and both sides claim Abraham. This chapter has hard words, spoken in a fierce argument among Jews, and over the centuries some Christians twisted those words into hatred of Jewish people, with terrible results. Churches today, Catholic and Protestant, have taught clearly against that reading. Then the line that ends the argument: "Before Abraham was, I am." Not before Abraham was, I was. I am. The same two Greek words as the voice on the water, ego eimi. The tenses don't match, and his listeners hear a claim to God's own name. They pick up stones, and he slips away. This week: bread of life, Peter's to whom shall we go, judging rightly at the feast of booths, belly, a stone set down, light, and now truth that frees.
